prompt: Which three things did Otávio say he needed from Renata?

choices.text: A weekly report of every ticket the team closed
choices.why: He had eleven teams; status was not what he asked for.

choices.text: No surprises
choices.why: Right: bad news from her before anybody else.

choices.text: That she solve problems without involving him
choices.why: He wanted problems brought to him, with options.

choices.text: Problems that come with options
choices.why: Right: with a recommendation, decided in five minutes.

choices.text: Her honest read of the team
choices.why: Right: including what was going badly.

prompt: Why does bad news that reaches a manager’s manager from somebody else cost so much?

choices.text: The news is worse when it comes second-hand
choices.why: The news is the same; what changes is what the silence implies.

choices.text: Company policy requires managers to report incidents within a day
choices.why: The lesson names no policy; the argument is about trust.

choices.text: He will then have to escalate it himself, to his own director, the same day
choices.why: Not the reason given.

choices.text: It raises the question of what else has not been told
choices.why: Right: the cost is to trust, not to the news itself.

prompt: Match each item from Renata’s one-to-one with Otávio to its kind.

pairs.left: "Two options for the Payments dependency; I recommend the second."
pairs.right: a decision she needs from him

pairs.left: "I’d like your view on how I handled the debrief."

prompt: Otávio twice committed Agenda to dates without asking Renata. What did she do?

choices.text: Raised it with his manager
choices.why: She went to him first, privately.

choices.text: Told the team the dates were his and not hers
choices.why: That turns a decision into a grievance, which the lesson warns against.

choices.text: Accepted it as part of the job
choices.why: Saying nothing teaches the team that feedback runs one way.

choices.text: Gave him feedback in private: the meetings, the effect, and what he would need to check first
choices.why: Right: the same structure as feedback downwards, and they agreed he would say he would confirm with her.

prompt: In Lencioni’s argument, who is a leader’s first team?
hint: Not the people who report to them.

choices.text: The people who report to them
choices.why: That is the natural view; Lencioni argues against it.

choices.text: Their peers, the other managers reporting to the same person
choices.why: Right: because most problems a manager cannot solve alone are between teams.

choices.text: Their own manager, and the directors above that manager, who set the priorities
choices.why: Not the claim.

choices.text: The product manager and designer working with the team
choices.why: Close collaborators, but not the claim.

prompt: What did the monthly coffee between Renata and Bia have on its agenda?

choices.text: The open items of the Payments dependency, reviewed in order
choices.why: The dependency was what led to it, not its agenda.

choices.text: Each team’s incidents from the month
choices.why: Not described.

choices.text: Headcount requests for the next quarter
choices.why: Not described.

choices.text: Nothing: it had no agenda
choices.why: Right: and it paid off in ways neither planned.

prompt: What changed in the fortnightly meeting of Otávio’s managers after Renata’s suggestion?

choices.text: It moved from fortnightly to weekly
choices.why: The cadence was not the problem.

choices.text: Each manager got a fixed five minutes to report
choices.why: That is the status format it replaced.

choices.text: It opened with problems crossing teams, and status became a written update read beforehand
choices.why: Right: the time together went on what needed the others in the room.

choices.text: Otávio stopped attending
choices.why: Not described.

prompt: Yara asked whether she would definitely be promoted if she led the migration. Why could Renata not promise it?

choices.text: The decision belonged to the panel
choices.why: Right: a promise would have been about somebody else’s decision.

choices.text: She thought Yara was not ready
choices.why: She believed Yara probably would be promoted.

choices.text: Caju forbids managers from discussing promotions with their reports
choices.why: She discussed it openly, just without a promise.

choices.text: The migration was not yet approved
choices.why: Not the reason given.

prompt: Put in order the shape of what Renata said instead of a promise.
trap: Ending on the action without a date leaves the person waiting with no end.

prompt: Somebody asks directly about a reorganisation you know of and cannot discuss. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: "There’s nothing going on."
choices.why: A lie that will be remembered, and every later reassurance discounted.

choices.text: "That’s not something I’m able to discuss."
choices.why: Right: honest, and respected more than people expect.

choices.text: Change the subject without answering, and raise it with your own manager afterwards
choices.why: Avoiding the question reads as an answer; say plainly you cannot discuss it.

choices.text: Share what you know in confidence
choices.why: You were asked not to; push for it to be shared early instead.

prompt: Each of Renata’s answers promises the manager’s own ____, which can be kept, and refuses to promise somebody else’s decision.
Fábio asks for a raise to match a friend’s offer. Which reply follows the lesson?
hint: An action of hers, with a date.

choices.text: "I’ll get you the raise."
choices.why: Not hers to give.

choices.text: "That isn’t something managers deal with."
choices.why: True of the bands, but it offers nothing she can do.

choices.text: "Your friend’s company pays more because it is riskier."
choices.why: Argues with the request instead of answering it.

choices.text: "Pay bands are set by the company. I’ll check where you sit and tell you what I find by the end of the month."
choices.why: Right: it promises her own action and a date, not the company’s decision.

prompt: Renata argued against a decision from above, and it went the other way. How does the lesson say she carries it to the team?

choices.text: Presenting it as her own idea
choices.why: That is dishonest about the disagreement.

choices.text: Explaining that it came from Otávio and that she disagreed, so the team knows whom to blame
choices.why: That turns it into a grievance, and leaves a team trusting nobody above.

choices.text: Holding it back from the team until she has had one more chance to change Otávio’s mind
choices.why: Not what the lesson describes.

choices.text: As the team’s decision, acknowledging her disagreement if asked
choices.why: Right: "I argued for something different, it went the other way, and here’s what we’re going to do."

prompt: Why does the lesson say a manager who never asks their own manager for help is not handling everything alone?
hint: What she is doing alone instead.

choices.text: Her manager is quietly handling the hard parts for her without ever telling her about it
choices.why: Not the argument.

choices.text: Her team carries the load
choices.why: Not the argument.

choices.text: Asking for help is part of the formal review
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: She is making the mistakes alone, and her manager finds out later
choices.why: Right: the third kind of item is the one new managers leave out.
